opus-5.5.text:
I think my background gave me a slightly different way of looking at problems. I didn't come up through the standard computer science pipeline of algorithms courses, systems, and competitive programming. My early training leaned more toward physics, mathematics, and the engineering view of signals and the physical world. For a long time I saw that as a gap I had to fill, and in some ways it was. I had to teach myself many things that CS students take for granted.

Over time I came to see it as a strength, especially in the areas I care about: 3D vision, robotics, and embodied intelligence. These fields aren't only about data and models. They're about the physical world: geometry, dynamics, contact, how objects actually move and interact. If you were trained to think from first principles about physical systems, you have an instinct for structure. You ask what is invariant here, what the underlying physics is, and what the model has to respect versus what it can learn from data.

People with formal CS training are often very strong at abstraction, scaling, and engineering large systems, and I deeply respect that. I've learned a lot from collaborators and students who are much better engineers than I am. My contribution is often a different question: not "how do we make this model bigger?" but "what is the right representation of the world for this problem?" In robotics that question matters a great deal, because data is expensive and the real world doesn't forgive you.

A second strength, I think, is comfort with being an outsider. When you enter a field from the side, you're less attached to its conventions. You don't automatically accept that a problem has to be framed a certain way. That gives you some freedom to try directions that insiders might think are unconventional, like using large-scale simulation and synthetic data to train robots, at a time when many people believed you must collect everything in the real world.

So I'd describe it as complementarity. I try to bring physical intuition and a first-principles mindset, and then work with people who have deep CS expertise to turn those ideas into systems that actually scale. The most interesting problems today, especially in embodied AI, sit right at that intersection.

fable-5.1.text:
I think my strength actually comes from the fact that I wasn't formally trained in computer science. My background is in physics, and physics trains you to think about problems from first principles rather than from the toolbox you happen to have.

When I came into AI and robotics, I didn't carry a lot of the assumptions that people with a traditional CS education take for granted. A lot of them had been taught a specific way of framing a problem, specific benchmarks to care about, specific architectures that were considered "correct." I didn't have that baggage, so I was more willing to ask naive questions. Sometimes naive questions turn out to be the important ones. Why does this representation have to be discrete? Why are we assuming the world is a set of labeled objects at all? A physicist is used to asking what the real variables of the system are, what is conserved, what is invariant under transformation. That way of thinking turned out to map very naturally onto problems like 3D perception and embodied AI, where geometry and symmetry really matter.

The second thing is tolerance for ambiguity. In physics you spend years working on problems where nobody tells you the answer exists. You learn to sit with a messy, ill-defined question and slowly shape it into something you can attack. Many well-trained engineers are extremely good once the problem is defined, but they're less comfortable in that earlier stage where you don't even know what the right question is. I enjoy that stage. I think a lot of the real value in research comes from problem selection, not problem solving.

Of course there are weaknesses too. I had to catch up on engineering fundamentals, on systems, on how to build things that actually run at scale. My students are often much better than me at that, and I rely on them. But I've come to believe that for a research leader, the deeper advantage is taste: knowing which direction is worth years of effort. That taste came from physics, and from being an outsider who had to build his own map instead of inheriting one.

astra-6.text:
I think my strengths are less about having the same technical foundation as someone formally trained in computer science and more about bringing a different perspective to a problem. I tend to start by asking: What are we actually trying to understand? Which assumptions matter? And is the way we’ve framed the question useful?

That doesn’t replace technical depth. There are areas where someone with formal training will be much stronger, and I need to learn from them. But research also involves choosing questions, connecting ideas, and recognizing when a familiar approach isn’t quite right. I see those as complementary strengths rather than a competition between backgrounds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my strength is probably more in how I frame a problem. Someone formally trained in computer science may have a much stronger foundation in algorithms and systems, and I respect that. I’m more inclined to start by asking: What are we actually trying to understand? Are we making the right assumptions? Is there another way to formulate the question?

Of course, that doesn’t replace technical depth. You still have to do the work and make your ideas precise. But I think you can contribute without having exactly the same strengths as everyone else. For me, the goal is to develop that perspective while continuing to learn from people whose technical foundations are stronger than mine.
